en: The Scripture on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts for Upāsakas, in one fascicle, translated by Guṇavarman during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. At that time, King Śuddhodana...
He approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to request something for my own deliverance."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately grant my wish!
The Buddha said, "This is a wish that can be granted; it shall be according to what you, O King, have requested!"
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, you have already established the light and heavy precepts for the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs. We only pray that the Tathāgata will likewise distinguish for us upāsakas which of the five precepts are subject to confession and which are not, so that we may recognize the characteristics of the precepts and be free from doubt.”
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent, Kauṇḍinya!
It has been my intention from the beginning that I long wished to explain the five precepts to the upāsakas.”
If there are good sons who receive and uphold [this teaching] without transgression, by these causes and conditions they shall attain the Buddha-way.
If there are those who transgress and do not repent, they will constantly remain within the three miserable realms.
At that time, after the Buddha had preached various teachings to King Śuddhodana, the king, having heard the Dharma, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.
On account of this, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now wish to explain to the upāsakas the gravity of offenses regarding the violation of precepts—those which are subject to repentance and those which are not.”
The bhikṣus all said:
"Indeed, we wish and desire to hear it!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are three ways of committing the offense of taking human life:
first, doing it oneself; second, commanding another to do it;
[and third, approving of its being done]."
Third is dispatching a messenger.
"Acting oneself" means taking another's life with one's own hand;
"instructing others" means speaking to another person, saying:
"Seize this man, bind him, and take his life.
He then dispatched a messenger to say to another person:
"Do you know such-and-such a person?"
“Seize this man, bind him, and take his life.
When the messenger takes that person’s life according to these instructions, the upāsaka commits an offense of irreparable transgression (*āpatti-ānantarya*).
Furthermore, there are three ways of taking human life: [text continues]
First, using internal form;
second, using non-internal form;
third, using both internal and non-internal form.
Regarding internal form: if a lay follower strikes another with his hand, or with his foot or any other part of his body, he forms this thought:
"May he die because of this!"
If the person dies as a result of that, one commits an offense of irreparable transgression (*āpatti-ānantarya*);
if they do not die immediately, but later die because of it, one likewise commits an offense of irreparable transgression;
if they do not die immediately, nor die later because of it, it is an intermediate offense that can be confessed.

Regarding "using that which is not internal form": suppose a person, with wood, tiles, stones, swords, spears, bows, arrows, white tin, lead ingots, or pieces of tin, hurls them from afar at another person, thinking:
"May he die because of this!"
If he dies because of that, he commits an offense of irreparable transgression;
if he does not die immediately but later dies as a result of it, he likewise commits an offense of irreparable transgression;
if he does not die immediately and later does not die as a result of it, it is an intermediate offense that may be confessed.

Regarding "using internal or external forms": if one takes hold of wood, tiles, stones, swords, spears, bows, arrows, white tin, lumps of lead, pieces of pewter, or pieces of wood with the hand and strikes another, forming this thought:
"May they die because of this!"
If the person dies because of that, the offense is irredeemable;
if they do not die immediately, but later die because of it, it is also an irredeemable offense;
if they do not die immediately, and later do not die because of it, it is a medium offense that can be redeemed.

Furthermore, there are those who, neither by means of internal matter, nor by means of non-internal matter, nor by means of both internal and non-internal matter, prepare various poisonous drugs for the purpose of killing someone. Whether these are applied to the eyes, ears, nose, or an ulcer on the body; or whether they are placed within various foods, bedding, or carriages—with the thought:
"May he die because of this!"
If the person dies because of it, one commits an offense of irreparable transgression;
if they do not die immediately, but die later as a result of this, one also commits an offense of irreparable transgression;
if they do not die immediately, nor die later as a result of this, it is an intermediate offense that may be confessed.

Furthermore, there are those who kill others by means of smokeless fire-pits, by crushing, by snares, by pits, by touch-killing, by *vidhara*-killing, by causing abortion, or by pressing on the abdomen; or they push them into fire or water, or push them into pits to kill them; or they dispatch them to travel along a road so that they die there; even down to the case where one initiates the means of killing while the fetus has first received its two faculties—the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*)—this constitutes killing by means of a smokeless fire-pit.
If an upāsaka knows that a person has come by this path, he first prepares a pit of smokeless fire within it and covers it with sand and soil;
then he says aloud: "Because this person has come by this path, I have prepared this pit."
If this person dies as a result of this [act], one commits an offense of non-expiation;
if they do not die immediately but die later as a result of it, one commits an offense of non-expiation;
if they do not die immediately and do not die later as a result of it, it is a middling offense that can be expiated.
If one creates a pit of smokeless fire for others, there is no repentance possible if a human being dies;
if a non-human being dies, it is a middle-grade offense that can be repented;
if an animal dies, it is a lower-grade offense that can be repented.
If one digs a pit for a non-human being and that non-human being dies, it is a middling offense that may be confessed;
if a human being dies, it is a minor offense that may be confessed;
if an animal dies, one commits a minor offense that may be confessed.
If one digs a pit for an animal and the animal dies, it is an offense of the lowest grade that may be confessed;
if a human falls and dies, or a non-human being falls and dies, in all such cases one commits an offense of the lowest grade that may be confessed.
If an upāsaka does not specifically intend for a pit to be made for a single purpose, but intends for all who come to fall into it and die: if a human dies, he commits an offense of non-expiation;
if a non-human dies, it is an intermediate offense of expiation;
if an animal dies, it is a minor offense of expiation.
There is no one who actually dies; rather, one incurs the three types of offenses involving preparatory effort that are subject to confession.
This is called "killing by means of a smokeless fire-pit.

Regarding the *vīdara*: if an upāsaka, on the twenty-ninth day of the month, seeks out the corpse of a person whose body is intact, summons spirits through mantras to cause the corpse to rise, washes it, clothes it, and causes its hands to grasp a sword, and then mentally intends or verbally declares:
Thinking, "For the sake of such-and-such a person, I shall perform this vidyā!
one then recites the incantation. If the intended victim is killed, it constitutes an offense of non-remorse (anivārya).

If the victim has entered various samādhis, or is protected by devas, or is rescued and released by a great master of mantras, and the harm is not accomplished, it constitutes an offense of intermediate remorse (madhyama-deśanīya).
This is called *vīdara*-killing. As for *ardha-vīdara*:

if an upāsaka, on the twenty-ninth day, constructs an iron chariot; having constructed the iron chariot, he constructs an iron man; he summons a spirit and casts a spell upon the iron man to cause it to rise; he washes it with water and clothes it; he causes the iron man to grasp a sword in his hand;
and if he thinks in his mind and speaks with his mouth: "I am reciting this mantra for the sake of [so-and-so]!"
"If this person dies, one commits an unforgivable offense;

if the other person has entered various samādhis, is protected by celestial deities, or is rescued and released by a master of mantras such that death does not occur, it is a middling offense that can be repented."
This is called the "Half-Vidala Killing.

Regarding the "Taking of Life": on the twenty-ninth day, one smears cow dung upon the ground, places wine and food therein, and having lit a fire, immediately casts it into water. Then, whether contemplating in the mind, speaking with the mouth, or reciting incantations, one says:
"May [the life] be extinguished as the fire is extinguished in the water."
"If the fire is extinguished, his life shall follow in extinction.
Furthermore, on the twenty-ninth day, cow dung was smeared upon the ground, wine and food were placed therein, and an image of the person intended for execution was drawn.
Having fashioned the image, he immediately strikes it down and extinguishes it; with mind and speech, he recites incantations, saying:
"As this image is extinguished, so too is that life extinguished."
"If the image perishes, his life shall perish accordingly.

Furthermore, on the twenty-ninth day, he smeared the ground with cow dung, placed wine and food upon it, and pierced the corner of a garment with a needle. He then immediately withdrew the needle while reciting incantations with his mind and voice, saying:
"As this needle comes out, his life shall come out accordingly."
This is called taking life.
If one uses various incantations to cause death, one commits an offense that cannot be remedied;
if the person does not die, it is a middling offense that can be remedied.

Furthermore, regarding those who cause abortion: they administer emetics or purgatives to women who are pregnant, or apply medicinal infusions to all parts of the body, or pierce the blood vessels, or even administer drugs that induce tears, with the thought:
"By these means and conditions, I shall cause the woman to die."
If the person dies, one commits an offense of non-expiation;
if they do not die immediately but later die as a result of this, one also commits an offense of non-expiation;
if they do not die immediately and later do not die as a result of this, it is an intermediate offense that may be expiated.
If one causes an abortion for the purpose of killing the mother, if the mother dies, it is an offense that cannot be atoned for;
if the fetus dies, this offense can be atoned for;
if both die, this offense cannot be atoned for.
If neither [the mother nor the fetus] dies, it is an intermediate offense that may be confessed.
If, for the purpose of killing the fetus, one employs a method to induce abortion and the fetus dies, one commits an unconceivable offense;
if the fetus does not die, it is an intermediate offense that may be confessed.
If only the mother dies, it is a grave offense that may be expiated;
if both die, it is an inexpiable transgression.
This is called the method for inducing abortion and killing.

"Pressing on the abdomen" means causing a pregnant woman to perform heavy labor or carry heavy loads, instructing her to run before a carriage, or making her climb a steep bank, while forming this thought:
"May this woman die."
If the person dies, it is an offense of non-remorse;
if they do not die immediately, but later die as a result of this, the offense is one of non-remorse;
if they do not die because of this, it is a middling offense that can be remedied through remorse.
If it concerns a fetus, as explained above, this is called "killing by pressing the abdomen.
As for "sending someone to die on the road," one knows that there are hungry wild beasts on that path; one sends them to that dangerous place with the thought:
"Let them die in those evil paths."
If the victim dies, one commits an offense of irreparable transgression;
for other cases, one also commits an offense, as explained above.
This is called killing within the evil realms.

Even while still in the mother’s womb, at the stage of the *kalala* when one first acquires two faculties—the body faculty and the life faculty—if one gives rise to a murderous intent and employs means to cause death; [this constitutes the offense].
If the person dies, one commits an offense of irreparable transgression;
for other offenses, they are the same as described above.
"There are three kinds of praising killing: [text continues]"
First, those who observe unwholesome precepts;
second, those who observe wholesome precepts;
third, those who are aged or ill.

Regarding those who observe evil precepts—such as those who slaughter oxen and sheep, raise chickens and pigs, release hawks to catch fish, hunt rabbits with nets or shoot deer and elk, act as thieves, bandits, or executioners, cast spells upon dragons, or serve as prison guards—if one approaches such people and speaks these words:
"You who observe evil precepts, why do you persist in committing such sins for so long?"
"It would be better to die early!
If a person dies because of this [thought], the offense cannot be expiated;
if they do not die because of it, it is a middling offense that can be expiated.
If an evil person says,
"I will not use this person's words," and does not die as a result,
one commits a middling offense requiring confession.
If, after praising this person so that they die, one feels regret in one's heart and thinks,
"Why did I instruct this person to die?
and returns to say:

"You evil persons, it may be that by means of the conditions of virtuous friends, you have drawn near to good people, heard the sublime Dharma, and been able to engage in correct reflection; thus you have become free from evil transgressions. You must not take your own lives."
"If a person accepts these words and does not die, this is a transgression that may be repented.
Those who observe the precepts well are the fourfold assembly of the Tathāgata."
If one encounters virtuous people, one should speak thus:
"O person who maintains the good precepts and possesses merit,
upon death you shall receive heavenly blessings."
"Why do you not take your own life?
If that person, because of this, commits suicide and dies, they commit an irredeemable offense;
if they do not kill themselves, it is a medium offense that can be atoned for.
If a person of virtuous precepts thinks,
"Why should I take my own life based on another's words?
and does not die, this offense can be expiated.
If, after instructing another to die, one feels regret and says:
"I was wrong! Why did I instruct this virtuous person to die?"
He returned and said to him:
"O you of virtuous precepts, as long as you remain alive, your merit will increase; because your merit increases, the blessings you receive will also increase, so do not take your own life."
"If one does not die because of this, the offense is grave and may be confessed.
Regarding those who are old or sick, whose four elements (mahābhūta) fluctuate and who undergo various sufferings and afflictions, one should go and say to such a person:
'Why do you endure this suffering for so long? Why do you not take your own life?'"
If the patient dies as a result, this offense cannot be expiated;
if they do not die as a result, it is a middling offense that can be expiated.
If the sick person thinks thus:
"Why should I follow this person's words and take my own life?
If, after speaking thus to the sick person, one feels regret in one's heart, thinking:
"This was not right!"
"Why do you tell these sick people to commit suicide?
He returned and said to them:

"You sick people, if you obtain good medicine and have caregivers who look after you well, and if you follow the prescribed diet and medication, your illnesses can be cured; do not take your own lives!"
"If death does not occur as a result, this constitutes an offense that may be confessed.
Regarding the remaining seven types of killing, the explanations of what constitutes an offense and what does not are the same as those for the fire pit above."
If one kills a human being while perceiving them as a human, this offense is unforgivable (*ānantarya*).
If one kills a non-human being while perceiving them as a human, or kills with doubt regarding whether they are a human, these all constitute unforgivable offenses.
If one kills a non-human being while perceiving them as a non-human, or kills with doubt regarding whether they are a non-human, these are offenses of intermediate gravity that may be expiated.

Furthermore, there was a man whose hands and feet had been severed and placed within the city moat. A great number of women entered the city and, hearing the sound of his wailing, went to see him for themselves. They said to one another:
"If someone could give this man a medicinal potion to drink so that he might die at once, he would not have to suffer for long!"
Among them was a simple-minded woman who gave her a medicinal potion, and she died immediately.
The other women said, "You have violated the precepts; there can be no repentance!"
He immediately informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If someone dies when you give them a medicinal decoction, you have committed an offense that cannot be expiated."
"If a layperson employs a means intending to kill his mother, but kills someone who is not his mother, this is a middling offense that may be confessed;

if a layperson intends to kill someone who is not his mother, but instead kills his own mother, this constitutes a middling offense that may be confessed, but it is not a pācittiya (an act of immediate retribution)."
"If a householder employs a means intending to kill a human being, but instead kills a non-human being, this is an offense of intermediate gravity that may be confessed;
if a householder employs a means intending to kill a non-human being, but instead kills a human being, he commits a minor offense that may be confessed."
"If a person conceives the fetus of an animal, and that fetus is aborted, one commits a minor offense requiring confession;
if an animal conceives the fetus of a human, and that fetus dies upon being aborted, one commits an offense not to be confessed."
"If a layperson prepares the means to kill someone, and the layperson dies first, and subsequently another person dies, this offense is expiable.
If a layperson intends to kill his parents and a doubt arises in his mind:
'Are these my parents?'"
"Is it not so? If one knows for certain that it was one's parents who killed them, this is a heinous crime (*ānantarya*) that cannot be expiated.
If a layperson gives rise to doubt, wondering whether it was a human or a non-human?
If one knows with certainty that this person is the culprit and kills them, it constitutes an offense of non-expiation (*anantarya*).
"If a person seizes a thief intending to kill him, but the thief manages to escape..."
If, by means of official power or the strength of a village, pursuers chase after these thieves, and a householder comes along the road in the opposite direction, the pursuers ask the householder:
"Have you seen the thieves?"
If this layperson previously harbored malice and resentment toward the thieves and says,
"I saw him at this place," thereby causing the thieves to lose their lives through these causes and conditions, he commits an offense of irreparable transgression.

Suppose a person is leading a large band of thieves intending to kill someone, and those thieves manage to escape; if the pursuers, whether by the power of the government or the power of the village, give chase, and a householder comes along the road and the pursuers ask him:
"Do you see the thieves?"
Among those thieves, there may be one person whom the householder hates, who says:
"I saw him at this place.
If he kills someone other than the one he hates, that offense is repentable.
The rest is as explained above.
"If one kills a non-mother while perceiving her to be one's mother, it constitutes an offense requiring confession (pāyattika), but it is not a grave offense (ānantarya).
If one strikes another in jest and the person dies, this offense may be confessed."
If one kills while insane and does not remember doing so, there is no offense.
If an upāsaka uses water containing insects, or kills insects among plants and trees, he commits an offense;
if he uses water thinking it contains insects when it is actually free of them, he likewise commits an offense.
If one perceives that there are no insects when there are insects, this also constitutes an offense.
There was a householder who had built a new dwelling and was staying on the roof; he dropped a beam from his hands, which fell upon the head of a carpenter, who died immediately.
The lay devotee gave rise to doubt, wondering,
"Is this offense capable of being expiated?
He questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is no offense.
Because there were few people on the roof to restrain it, the beam fell onto the carpenter's head and killed him.
The householder immediately became suspicious.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, apply yourself with a good mind and do not allow anyone to be killed!"
"Furthermore, another householder was working on the roof when he saw a scorpion in the mud. Terrified, he leaped down and fell upon a carpenter, who died instantly.
The householder became suspicious."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, apply yourself with care in your work and do not allow anyone to be killed!"

"Furthermore, there was another householder who, at dusk, entered a dangerous path and encountered bandits. When the bandits sought to seize him, he abandoned them and fled, falling onto a weaver beneath a cliff edge; the weaver died immediately."
The layperson immediately became suspicious.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"Furthermore, there was another householder who pushed a rock down from a mountain; the rock fell and killed a person, leading him to harbor doubts.
The Buddha said:
'There is no offense.'"
When one wishes to push down a stone, one should first cry out,
"Beware of the falling stone!
so that others may take notice.
"Furthermore, there was another man who had a boil that had not yet ripened; a householder lanced it for him, and the man died. He immediately gave rise to doubt.
The Buddha said:
'If a boil has not yet ripened and a person dies because it was lanced, this is an offense that may be confessed.'"
"If one dies from bursting a ripe boil or ulcer, there is no offense.
Furthermore, a young child was laughing; a householder seized him and tickled him until he laughed so hard that he died.
The lay devotee became doubtful.
The Buddha said,
"Because it was done in jest, there is no offense of killing."
"From now on, you must not tickle others to make them laugh.
Another person sat there covering himself with his robe.
The householder called out to him:
"Get up! The man said:
"Do not call me; if I get up, I shall die."
He called out again,
"Get up! and as soon as he rose, he died.
The lay devotee became doubtful.
The Buddha said:
"You have committed an offense that is confessable."
The Second Precept on Stealing: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"An upāsaka commits an offense of irreparable retribution by taking another's property of significant value in three ways:
first, through the application of intent;..."
Second, the employment of the body;
third, departing from one's original location.
Regarding the employment of the mind: it is the arousal of thought and reflection with the intent to commit theft.
"Regarding 'using the body,' it means taking another's property by means of one's own limbs or other parts;
regarding 'moving from its original place,' it means lifting the object from wherever it lies and placing it elsewhere.
Furthermore, there are three ways of taking another's valuable property that constitute an offense of irreparable transgression:"
First, taking it oneself;
second, instructing another to take it;
third, sending a messenger to take it.
"To take by oneself" means to lift it with one's own hand and move it from its original place;
"to instruct another to take" refers to if a lay follower (upāsaka) instructs someone, saying:
"Steal another's property."
When that person takes it at will and moves it from its original place,
he sends a messenger and says to the agent:
"Do you know where that heavy object is?"
He replied, "I know its location.
He was then sent to steal it; as the man followed these instructions and took it away from its original place, [the offense was committed].
"Furthermore, there are five ways of taking another's valuable property that constitute an offense of non-expiation:
first, taking by means of harsh coercion;
second, taking through contemptuous disregard;"
Third, taking by falsely assuming another's name;
fourth, taking by forceful seizure;
fifth, taking what has been entrusted to one.
Regarding "valuable objects": if they consist of five *kārsāpaṇas* or items worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, one commits an offense that cannot be remedied (*anivārya*).

If a layperson knows that another possesses the five treasures or items resembling them, and with a thieving mind selects them but has not yet removed them from their place, one commits an offense that can be remedied (*sāvadya*).
If, having made a selection, one takes [an object] away from its original location when it is worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, one commits an offense that cannot be rectified.
Regarding "removed from its original location": if it is a woven cloth, a change in the threads constitutes a different location;
if it is leather or clothing, being of a single color constitutes one location, while being of different colors constitutes different locations.
Regarding leather garments, those of a single color are called one place, while those of different colors are called different places;

regarding woolen rugs, a single layer of wool is called one place, and a single color is called one place, while different colors are called different places—these are what are termed "various places."

When a layperson carries goods for another, if with a thieving mind they shift them from the left shoulder to the right shoulder, or move them from the right hand to the left hand—such bodily movements are termed "moving to another place."

In a carriage, there are the wheels, axles, crossbars, and yokes; on a boat, there are the two sides, the bow, and the stern; in a house, there are the beams, ridgepoles, rafters, corner-posts, and inner recesses—all of these have distinct names for their respective locations.
"To move objects with a thieving mind and place them in various other locations constitutes an offense of irreparable transgression (*āpatti-pārājika*).

Regarding the theft of objects in water: if a person’s raft or timber is being carried downstream by the current, and a householder takes it with a thieving mind, he commits an offense of irreparable transgression."

If, with a mind of theft, one seizes a piece of wood and holds it stationary, and it subsequently drifts toward the upper limit [of the water], or if, with a mind of theft, one sinks it to the bottom and then lifts it out of the water, in all such cases, one commits an offense that cannot be remedied.

"Furthermore, if one presses a bird being raised in a pond owned by another into the water with a thieving intent, one commits an offense that may be confessed; if one lifts it out of the water, one commits an offense that cannot be confessed."

If someone raises birds at home, and they fly into a wild pond, if one, with a thieving mind, picks them up and removes them from the water, or causes them to sink to the bottom, in all such cases one commits an offense of irreparable transgression.

Furthermore, if there is a layperson whose articles of internal and external adornment are atop a multi-storied pavilion, and various birds that have owners carry these items away, one who seizes them from those birds with a thieving mind commits an offense of irreparable transgression.
If one sees a bird flying while carrying a jewel and, with a thieving mind, waits for it from afar, one commits an offense that is confessable as a middling transgression (*madhyama-deśanīya*).
If, by the power of incantations, one causes the bird to go wherever it desires, one commits an offense that is not to be confessed (*anāpatti*);
if it goes elsewhere, one commits a confessable offense as a middling transgression.
If a wild bird carries off a jewel and departs, and a lay practitioner seizes it from the bird with the intent to steal, he commits an offense of intermediate expiation;
while waiting for the wild bird, he commits an offense of minor expiation.

Furthermore, if various wild birds carry off jewels and depart, and a bird with an owner seizes them from the wild birds, and a householder, with a mind of theft, seizes them from the bird with an owner, he commits an offense that is not to be confessed;
if he waits for the bird [to act], he commits an intermediate offense that is to be confessed.
The rest is as explained above.

Furthermore, if a bird possessing a master takes a precious object in its beak and it is seized by a wild bird, and a lay devotee (gṛhapati), with the intent to steal, seizes it from the wild bird and takes it, he commits an offense of intermediate expiation (sthūlātyaya);
if he waits for the bird [to leave], he likewise commits an offense of intermediate expiation.
The rest is also as above.
"If a householder, while gambling, uses a deceitful mind to shift the dice and defeats another to obtain five coins, he commits an offense of non-expiation.
If a householder steals a relic with a thieving mind, he commits an offense of intermediate expiation."
If one forms this thought with a respectful mind,
"The Buddha is also my teacher," and takes [the object] with a pure mind, there is no offense.
If a layperson takes a scripture with a thieving mind, they commit an offense that cannot be rectified; the gravity of the offense is determined by the value of the object.
Now, regarding those who steal fields, there are two causes and conditions for seizing another's land:
first, verbal dispute.
Second, regarding the act of making a sign:

if a layperson, for the sake of land, says that another has won, yet makes a false sign and thereby obtains more land than his share—provided the value of the land is five coins or more—he commits an offense of irreparable transgression.
“There are some householders who, being liable to pay customs duties, do not pay them; if the value reaches five coins, they commit an offense of non-expiation.
Furthermore, there are householders who go to a customs station and say to other householders:
‘Carry these goods across for me, and I will give you half the duty.’”
Regarding "one who carries it past [the checkpoint]": if one evades a tax of five *kārsāpaṇas*, one commits an offense that cannot be remedied.
If a householder shows another person a different route so as to cause them to lose the taxable goods, and the value of those goods is five *kārsāpaṇas*, one commits an offense that can be remedied.
If there are bandits, wild beasts, or famine at a place of taxation, and one intentionally shows a different path to avoid such harm, there is no offense.

Furthermore, if a layperson conspires with bandits to plunder villages and, upon obtaining goods, shares a portion worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, he commits an offense of irreparable transgression (*pārājika*).

Regarding the theft of legless sentient beings, such as leeches, *yutou* insects, *luochong* insects, and the like: if a person takes them from their vessel and places them therein, and a householder then takes them from that vessel, he commits an offense of non-expiation (*āpatti-āvaśeṣa*).
The selection is as stated above.

Regarding the theft of two-legged or three-legged sentient beings—such as humans, geese, swans, parrots, and other birds—if one takes them with a thieving mind while they are confined within a cage or enclosure, it constitutes an offense that cannot be remedied;
the rest is as explained above.
"There are two kinds of stealing:
first, carrying it away;
second, meeting by appointment."

If a layperson, with a thieving mind, carries another person upon their shoulder such that both of that person's feet leave the ground, they commit an offense of irreparable transgression (*āpatti-pārājika*);
if they travel together by prior agreement and exceed two *krośas*, they commit an offense of irreparable transgression;
all other cases are as explained above.
Regarding the theft of four-footed animals— namely elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep—

if a person ties them with a rope to one place and, with the intent to steal, pulls them so that they pass the distance of four *krośas*, it constitutes an offense of irreparable transgression (*pārājika*).
If one is lying in a single location and, with a thieving mind, drives them up and they pass four *krośas*, it constitutes an offense of non-expiation;
the same applies if there are many feet [of beings].
If they are within a wall, a fence, or a screen, and one, with a thieving mind, drives them out and they pass the group of four *krośas*, it constitutes an offense of non-expiation.
The rest is as explained above.
If it is released outside, the householder thinks with a mind of theft:
"When the herdsman enters the forest and departs, I shall steal it."
If the impulse to commit the act arises, it is an offense that can be confessed.
However, if one actually kills, one incurs the same guilt as the killer; having killed and taken meat worth five coins, one commits an offense that cannot be confessed.
"Furthermore, there are seven kinds:
first, the perception that it is not one's own;
second, lack of consent;"
Third, not using it even for a moment;
fourth, knowing there is an owner;
fifth, not being insane.
Sixth, not being mentally distracted;
seventh, not having a mind impaired by illness.
These seven [conditions], when taking a heavy object, constitute an offense of non-atonement.
To take light objects constitutes an offense of the middle grade that requires confession.
Furthermore, there are seven types [of such offenses]:
first, taking what one perceives as one's own;...
Second, with consent;
third, temporary use;
fourth, that which has no owner.
Fifth, insanity;
sixth, mental derangement;
seventh, a mind impaired by disease.
Regarding these seven cases, taking objects constitutes no offense.
There was a householder who planted radishes. Then another person came to the garden and said to the householder, "Give me some radishes."
The householder asked,
"Do you have a price, or do you simply demand it outright?
He replied:
"I have no price," [the monk] said.
The householder replied,
"If you require radishes, you should bring the price with you."
"If I were to give it to you alone, how could I provide for my morning and evening meals?
The guest said,
"Then you will certainly not give it to me!"
The host said,
"How could I give it to you! Thereupon,
the guest used a spell to cause the vegetables to wither and dry up.
He turned back, giving rise to doubt within himself:
"Could it be that I have committed an offense that cannot be remedied?
He went to the Tathāgata to resolve his uncertainty.
The Buddha said:
"In calculating the value of what has been transgressed—whether it be an offense that can be repented or one that cannot—the stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all the same as the root.
At that time, there was a man tilling the soil within the Jetavana Monastery; he had taken off his clothes and laid them aside on one side of the field.
At that time, there was a householder who, seeing no one when looking in the four directions, took the garment and departed.
A plowman saw him from afar and said to the householder,
"Do not take my garment!"
The householder did not hear this and, still thinking there was no owner, took the garment and departed.
The plowman immediately followed him and seized him, saying to the householder:
"According to your own law, is it not forbidden to take what is not given?"
The householder replied,
"I took it because I thought there was no owner;
how could the Dharma permit such a thing?"
The plowman said, "This is my garment.
The householder said:
"This is your robe; you may take it with you.
The householder became suspicious, thinking:
"Might I have committed an offense that is not to be confessed?"
He immediately went to where the Buddha was to inquire about this matter.
Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you take it?"
The householder replied,
"I said it had no owner.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.

From this day forward, those who take things must exercise careful deliberation. Even if there is no one guarding it, that which belongs to oneself, or that which actually has an owner even if unguarded, constitutes a minor offense of regrettable transgression (*pāyattika*) if one forms the intention to steal but does not yet take it;

it constitutes a middling offense of regrettable transgression if one takes it but the value is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*; and it constitutes an irredeemable offense (*pārājika*) if one takes it and the value reaches five *kārsāpaṇas*."
The Third Precept on Sexual Conduct: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "An upāsaka should not give rise to thoughts of desire or sensual perceptions;
he should not even allow such thoughts to arise in his mind, let alone give rise to the roots of unwholesome karma—the impurities of desire, hatred, delusion, and the fetters."
Within this, there are four objects for the commission of sexual misconduct:
males, females, eunuchs, and those with dual sexual organs.
As for "females," these include human females, non-human females, and female animals.
Regarding males, these include human males, non-human males, and male animals.
Eunuchs and those with dual sexual organs are likewise categorized as above.
"If an upāsaka commits sexual misconduct with a human female, a non-human female, or a female animal through the three [unlawful] passages, he commits an offense that cannot be rectified."
If one engages in sexual intercourse with a human male, a non-human male, a male animal, a eunuch, or a hermaphrodite at two locations, one commits an offense that cannot be remedied.
If one forms the intention to engage in sexual intercourse but the union does not occur, one commits a minor offense that can be remedied;
if the two bodies have united but one desists without engaging in intercourse, one commits a middling offense that can be remedied.
"If an upāsaka commits sexual misconduct with a female servant who has already been married off and has a husband, he commits an offense that cannot be rectified;
other minor offenses are as explained above."

"Regarding the three locations: the mouth, the anus, and the urinary tract. Apart from these three locations, engaging in sexual desire in any other place constitutes an offense that may be confessed.

If an upāsaka engages in unchaste conduct with a female servant who has not yet been married, by means of an improper path, he commits an offense that may be confessed; however, the retribution he shall suffer in future lives will be heavy."
"If an upāsaka has male servants or laborers and engages in sexual intercourse with them in the two [orifices], he commits an offense of irreparable transgression;
other minor offenses are as explained above."
"If an upāsaka engages in sexual intercourse with a prostitute and does not pay the fee, he commits the offense of sexual misconduct, which cannot be expiated;
if he pays the fee, there is no offense."

"If a person dies, or even if an animal dies, as long as the faculty of the body has not yet decayed, if one commits sexual misconduct with them—specifically in the case of a woman, committing it in the three places constitutes an irredeemable offense;
minor offenses are as explained above."

"If an upāsaka personally undertakes the eight precepts and engages in sexual intercourse, he commits an offense that cannot be rectified; as there is no distinction between 'wrong' and 'right' regarding these eight precepts, he has violated them all."

"If an upāsaka, although he has not received any precepts at all, violates one who observes the pure precepts of a disciple of the Buddha, then even though he incurs no offense for breaking precepts himself, he shall never thereafter be able to receive the five precepts or go forth to receive full ordination."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I have two bodies:
the physical body and the precept-body."

If a son of good family were to erect a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels for my physical body reaching as high as the Brahma Heaven, yet someone were to damage it, the sin of that person could still be repented;
however, to damage my body of precepts is a sin of immeasurable magnitude, leading to retribution like that of the Dragon King Elāpattra!
The Fourth Precept on False Speech: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "I have criticized false speech in various ways and praised those who do not speak falsely;

one should not even speak falsely in jest, much less intentionally. Regarding the transgression herein: if an upāsaka, without knowing or seeing the supramundane noble Dharma, says of himself, 'I am a candidate for arhatship' or 'I am an arhat.'"
One who says this commits an offense that cannot be rectified.
If one says:
"I am an Anāgāmin, a Sakṛdāgāmin, a Srotāpanna, or even one who is practicing toward the stage of Srotāpanna."

If one attains the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, or the fourth dhyāna; if one attains the immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; if one attains the formless attainments—the concentration of infinite space, the concentration of infinite consciousness, the concentration of nothingness, and the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; or if one attains the contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti)—then the devas will come to me, and the nāgas, yakṣas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and rākṣasas will come to me.
They will question me and I will answer them; I will question them and they will answer me.
In all such cases, one commits an offense that cannot be remedied.
If one originally intended to say "Arhat" but mistakenly said "Anāgāmin," one commits an offense that can be remedied through confession; the same applies to other such offenses.

"If a lay follower (upāsaka) is asked by someone, 'Have you attained the Path?', and he remains silent or indicates it through physical gestures, he commits an offense of the middle grade that requires confession. This applies even if he says, 'A whirlwind or an earth-dwelling spirit has come to my place'; he commits an offense of the middle grade that requires confession."

If an upāsaka hears something but says he did not hear it, sees something but says he did not see it, suspects its existence but says it does not exist, or says it exists when it does not—such false speech constitutes an offense that must be confessed.
If one gives rise to the intention to speak falsely, but has not yet spoken, one commits an offense of minor expiation;
if one speaks but does not express the full intent, one commits an offense of middling expiation.
If one declares to others that one has attained the Way, one commits an offense of inexpiable transgression.
"If one speaks while insane or mentally deranged and unaware of what is being said, there is no offense.

The Fifth Precept on Alcohol: The Buddha was staying at the town of Bhaddavatikā in the kingdom of Ceti. In that place there was a wicked dragon named Ambatittha, who was fierce, violent, and harmful; no one could reach his location. Elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, donkeys, mules, and camels were unable to approach him, and even birds could not fly over him.
When the autumn grain was ripe, it destroyed all other grains.

The Elder Śāṇakavāsin was traveling through the country of Caitya and gradually arrived at Bhadravatī. Having passed that night, at dawn he dressed, took his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food.

While begging for alms, he heard that in this town there was a malevolent dragon named Āmrapālī, who was fierce and cruel; neither people nor birds and beasts could go to his dwelling place, and whenever the autumn grain ripened, he would destroy it all.
Having heard this, after finishing his almsround, he went to the edge of the spring at the dwelling place of the dragon Āmrapālī and sat down upon a prepared seat.
When the dragon smelled the scent of his robes, he immediately gave rise to anger and emitted smoke from his body.
The Elder Śāgata immediately entered samādhi, and by means of his supernormal powers, smoke also issued from his body.
The dragon became even more enraged and emitted fire from its own body; Śāgata then again entered the Fire-Light Samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), and fire also issued from his body.
The dragon again rained down hail, but Śāgata immediately transformed the hail into *śikṣu* cakes, marrow cakes, and *pippala* cakes.
The dragon again released thunderbolts, which Śāgata transformed into various kinds of *mudga* (joy) cakes.
The dragon again rained down arrows, bows, swords, and spears, but Śāgata immediately transformed them into *utpala*, *padma*, and *kumuda* flowers.

Then the dragon again rained down poisonous snakes, centipedes, earth-vipers, and millipedes; Śāgata immediately transformed them into garlands of *utpala* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *vārṣika* flowers, and *atimuktaka* flowers.
All such powers possessed by these nāgas were manifested toward Śāgata.
Having thus displayed their virtues, because they could not prevail, they immediately lost their majestic power and radiance.

The Elder Śāṇakavāsin, knowing that the dragon’s power and strength were exhausted and that it could no longer move, immediately transformed his body into a minute form, entered through the dragon’s two ears, and emerged from its two eyes.
Having emerged from both eyes, they entered through his nose and exited through his mouth; they moved back and forth, pacing upon the dragon’s head without harming its body.
When the dragon witnessed these events, his heart was greatly startled, his hair stood on end with terror, and he joined his palms toward the Elder Śāgata and said:
“I take refuge in you!”
Śāgata replied: "Do not take refuge in me!
You should take refuge in my teacher; you should take refuge in the Buddha."
The dragon said, "From this day forth, I take refuge in the Triple Gem; know me as a lay disciple (*upāsaka*) of the Buddha for as long as my life lasts!

Having received the three refuges and become a disciple of the Buddha, the dragon no longer committed such violent and evil deeds as before. Humans, birds, and beasts were all able to reach his dwelling, and when the autumn grain ripened, he no longer damaged it. Thus, his reputation spread throughout all the lands.

The Elder Śākata was able to subdue the malevolent dragon, taming it to become virtuous; consequently, humans and birds and beasts were able to reach the dragon palace, and when the autumn grain ripened, it was no longer damaged.
Because the reputation of the Elder Kassapa had spread far and wide, people all invited him by sending food.

Among them was a poor woman who, out of faith and reverence, invited the Elder Kassapa. After Kassapa accepted her invitation in silence, the woman prepared for him a famous offering of milk-rice with ghee; he accepted it and ate it.
The woman thought to herself,
"If this śramaṇa eats this rice gruel made with *nāma-sarpis* and milk, it might cause him to suffer from a cold ailment.
She then took some wine that appeared like water and offered it to him.
Śāgata did not look at the drink.
Having drunk it, he preached the Dharma to him and departed, heading toward the monastery.

At that moment, the effects of the alcohol took hold; near the monastery gate, he fell prostrate on the ground. His saṃghāṭī robe and other garments, his water-strainer, bowl, staff, oil-sack, leather sandals, and needle-case were each in one place, while his body lay in another; intoxicated, he was unconscious of anything.
At that time, the Buddha was wandering with Ānanda and arrived at this place. Seeing this bhikṣu, the Buddha, though already knowing the answer, asked intentionally:
"Ānanda, who is this person?"
He replied,
“World-Honored One,
this is the Elder Śāgata.”
The Buddha then said to Ānanda, "Prepare a seat for me at this place, provide water, and assemble the Saṃgha.
Having received these instructions, Ānanda immediately prepared the seat, provided the water, and assembled the Saṃgha; he then went to inform the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"I have already spread the mats, prepared the water, and assembled the Saṃgha.
The Buddha, knowing the proper time himself, washed his feet and sat down, then asked the bhikṣus:

"Have you ever seen or heard of a dragon named Ambatittha, who is fierce, violent, and harmful? Previously, no human has ever reached his dwelling; neither elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, donkeys, mules, nor camels can go there. Not even birds dare to pass over him. When the autumn grain ripens, he destroys all the crops."
"Good son! Śāgata is able to subdue them and bring them to goodness; now these people and birds and beasts have reached the spring.
At that time, someone among the crowd who had seen it said:
“I have seen it, World-Honored One!
The hearer said:
“I have heard it, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "What do you think?
Is this son of good family, Śāṅghāta, able now to subdue the frog?
He replied:
“Impossible,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“If even the sages suffer such failings when they drink alcohol, how much more so for ordinary worldly people!
If there are transgressions beyond these, they all arise because of drinking alcohol.”
From this day forward, if you claim to be a disciple of the Buddha, you must not drink alcohol—not even a single drop on the tip of a blade of grass. You must not drink it at all.
After the Buddha had thus rebuked the faults of drinking liquor in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two kinds of liquor that an upāsaka must not drink: grain-based liquor and wood-based liquor."

As for wooden liquor, it may be made from roots, stems, leaves, flowers, or fruits; using various seeds and diverse medicinal herbs mixed together to create a liquor whose color, fragrance, and flavor can intoxicate those who drink it—this is what is called "liquor."
If an upāsaka swallows [the alcohol], it is also termed "drinking" and constitutes an offense.
If he drinks grain-based liquor (surā), he commits an offense with every swallow;
if he drinks fermented vinegar-based liquor (maireya), he commits an offense with every swallow.
If one drinks sweet wine, one commits an offense with every swallow.
If one eats yeast that can cause intoxication, one commits an offense with every swallow;
if one eats dregs of wine, one commits an offense with every swallow.
If one drinks the dregs of alcohol, one commits an offense with every swallow;
if one drinks that which resembles alcohol in color, fragrance, or taste, and is capable of intoxicating a person, one commits an offense with every swallow.
"If one merely produces the color of liquor, but it lacks the fragrance of liquor and the taste of liquor, such that it cannot intoxicate oneself or others, drinking it constitutes no offense.
*The Scripture on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts for Upāsakas*, translated by the Buddha, one fascicle.
